He takes the loss upon himself (Isaiah 53:4–6). Jacob bore Laban’s losses under compulsion; Christ bore ours willingly, out of love (John 10:17–18). The comparison is not exact, but it helps us see the character of a shepherd who absorbs the cost of others’ harm.

For anyone serving under unfair terms, Jacob’s example teaches patient endurance without bitterness, while also showing that it is not wrong to name injustice when the time comes to speak.

wordNotes.term: טְרֵפָה (terefah) — that which was torn of beasts
wordNotes.explanation: An animal killed or mangled by a predator. The law later forbade Israelites to eat such meat and released a keeper from liability if he brought the torn carcass as evidence. Jacob was denied that customary protection.

wordNotes.term: אֲחַטֶּנָּה (’achattennah) — I bare the loss of it
wordNotes.explanation: From the verb chata’, normally “to sin” or “miss the mark,” here used in an intensive form meaning “to bear the loss” or “to make good a shortfall.” Jacob made up from his own goods what was missing. The same verb, in other contexts, describes purification and the removal of sin by sacrifice.

verses.bibleText: Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob paints a vivid picture of a shepherd’s life: “Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.” In the uplands of Mesopotamia, days could be scorching and nights bitterly cold. A shepherd responsible for a flock could not retreat indoors when the weather turned. He stayed in the field, exposed, watchful, sleepless.

The word translated “drought” refers to intense heat, the dry burning of the day. The word for “frost” means cold or ice. Jacob suffered both extremes, often within a single day. The phrase “my sleep departed from mine eyes” shows how the demands of guarding sheep from predators and thieves kept him awake through the night watches. This was no easy job, and Jacob had done it for twenty years.

The verse has become one of the classic descriptions of faithful shepherding in Scripture. When Hosea recalled Jacob’s history he wrote, “Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep” (Hosea 12:12), remembering both the cost and the devotion of that service. The shepherd’s life of exposure and vigilance became an image of the care God expects from those who lead his people (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2–4).

Above all, Jacob’s sleepless watch points forward to Christ, the Good Shepherd. Jesus contrasted the hireling, who flees when the wolf comes because he does not care for the sheep, with the true shepherd who lays down his life for them (John 10:11–13). Jacob was technically a hired man, yet he served like an owner, bearing heat and cold for a flock that was not his. Christ went further still. He spent nights in prayer on mountainsides, endured weariness and thirst, and finally gave himself up on the cross so that his flock might live. The psalmist says of God, “He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). What Jacob did imperfectly and under compulsion, the Shepherd of Israel does perfectly and in love.

Pastors, parents, and all who carry responsibility for others may find in Jacob’s words a description of faithful care: present in the heat, present in the cold, awake when others sleep.

wordNotes.explanation: Chorev means dry heat, the burning of the sun; qerach means cold, frost, or ice. Set side by side, they express the full range of exposure a shepherd endured. Both words appear in Job’s descriptions of God’s power over weather.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּדַּד שְׁנָתִי (wattiddad shenati) — my sleep departed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nadad means to flee or wander away. Sleep is pictured as fleeing from Jacob’s eyes. A related expression describes the king’s sleepless night in Esther and the sleepless restlessness of the troubled.

verses.bibleText: Thus have I been twenty years in thy house; I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob sums up his account in numbers: “Thus have I been twenty years in thy house; I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.”

The arithmetic is pointed. Fourteen years of unpaid labor bought his wives; six years under constantly shifting terms produced his flock. Jacob does not mention the trick Laban played with Leah, perhaps out of consideration for Leah herself, who was listening. He simply states the cost. His years in Laban’s house were years of service in the full sense, the word often used for a servant’s or slave’s labor.

The repetition of “ten times” from verse 7 shows that this was a settled grievance. Whatever Laban promised, he did not keep. Jacob’s life had been governed by an employer who rewrote the rules whenever they favored the worker.

The word “served” has a long future in Scripture. Israel would later serve in Egypt with rigor (Exodus 1:13–14), and God would deliver them so that they might serve him instead (Exodus 4:23). Jacob’s twenty years of bitter service in Haran anticipate that larger story. The God who brought Jacob out of Laban’s house would bring his descendants out of Pharaoh’s. Paul would later contrast the bondage of sin with the freedom of serving God, whose wages are not changed and whose gift is eternal life (Romans 6:22–23).

wordNotes.explanation: From ‘avad, “to work, serve,” the root of the word for servant or slave. The verb can describe labor for a master, the bondage of Egypt, or the worship of God. Jacob’s choice of the word stresses that his time with Laban was a form of servitude.

verses.bibleText: Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob’s speech reaches its climax with a confession of faith: “Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty.” He knows that his prosperity is not ultimately the fruit of his labor or his shrewdness. Without God’s presence, Laban would have stripped him of everything and sent him home with nothing.

Jacob names God in three ways. “The God of my father” links him to Isaac’s faith. “The God of Abraham” reaches back to the founder of the family and the covenant promises. “The fear of Isaac” is a unique title, found only here and in verse 53. It may mean “the One whom Isaac feared,” the God Isaac revered and worshiped, or it may describe God as the awe-inspiring One who caused dread in Isaac’s enemies. Either way, it points to the living reality of God in Isaac’s experience. Isaac had lain bound on the altar at Moriah, and he had known God’s faithfulness through famine and conflict over wells. For Jacob, Isaac’s God was not an abstraction but a presence to be reckoned with. Laban had felt that presence in his dream the night before.

“God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands.” These words anticipate the burning bush, where God tells Moses, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people” (Exodus 3:7), and Israel’s confession at the offering of firstfruits, which recalls how the LORD “looked on our affliction, and our labour, and our oppression” (Deuteronomy 26:7). Jacob’s experience in Haran is a miniature of Israel’s later experience in Egypt.

“And rebuked thee yesternight.” Jacob interprets Laban’s dream as a divine verdict. The same verb used in verse 37 for the kinsmen judging between the parties is used here of God. The case has already been decided in the highest court. God has heard the evidence and ruled for Jacob.

The verdict, however, did not mean God endorsed every scheme Jacob had used. Protection is not the same as approval. Scripture elsewhere counsels the wronged not to repay evil for evil but to leave vengeance to God (Proverbs 20:22; Romans 12:17–19). Jacob was spared because God had chosen him and was faithful to his promise, and in his grace God would continue to reshape Jacob’s character through the struggle that lay ahead at the Jabbok.

wordNotes.term: פַּחַד יִצְחָק (pachad Yitschaq) — the fear of Isaac
wordNotes.explanation: Pachad means dread, terror, or awe. As a title for God it occurs only here and in verse 53. It likely means the God whom Isaac revered with holy awe, and perhaps also the God who brings dread upon those who oppose his people. Isaiah later calls on Israel to make the LORD their fear and their dread.

An adverb meaning “empty-handed” or “without anything.” God later commanded that a freed Hebrew servant was not to be sent away empty, and promised that Israel would not leave Egypt empty. Laban would have violated that principle had God not intervened.

verses.bibleText: And Laban answered and said unto Jacob, These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these cattle are my cattle, and all that thou seest is mine: and what can I do this day unto these my daughters, or unto their children which they have born?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban has no answer to Jacob’s case. He does not deny any of the charges, nor does he apologize. Instead he falls back on a claim of ownership: “These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these cattle are my cattle, and all that thou seest is mine.”

The fourfold “my” is breathtaking. After twenty years, after Jacob had paid for his wives with fourteen years of labor, after the flocks had been earned under terms Laban himself set and repeatedly changed, Laban still claims it all. His possessiveness runs so deep that he cannot conceive of his daughters as Jacob’s wives or of the flocks as Jacob’s wages. Everything in sight is his.

Yet his next words admit defeat: “and what can I do this day unto these my daughters, or unto their children which they have born?” The claim of ownership is empty. He can do nothing, because God has forbidden him. The question may also carry a hint of real paternal feeling. Whatever his faults, Laban did not wish harm to his own daughters and grandchildren. Even so, he frames it as though Jacob owed him gratitude for his restraint.

Laban’s boast resembles other empty claims in Scripture. The king of Sodom offered Abram goods that Abram had won back for him (Genesis 14:21). Satan offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world, as though they were his to give (Luke 4:6). Those who grasp tightly at what does not belong to them often speak most loudly of ownership.

The believer is reminded of the true owner of all things. “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). Neither Laban nor Jacob owned the flocks in the ultimate sense; God had given them. Recognizing God’s ownership frees us from Laban’s grasping spirit and teaches us to hold what we have as stewards.

wordNotes.term: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּה רֹאֶה לִי־הוּא (kol ’asher-’attah ro’eh li-hu’) — all that thou seest is mine
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “everything you are seeing, it is mine.” The emphatic placement of “mine” underlines Laban’s possessiveness. The words contrast with God’s claim in the psalms that every beast of the forest and the cattle on a thousand hills belong to him.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou; and let it be for a witness between me and thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Unable to win his case, Laban proposes a treaty: “Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou; and let it be for a witness between me and thee.” The man who came to seize now asks for a formal agreement.

The proposal is an admission. Laban recognizes that Jacob is no longer a servant in his household but the head of an independent family with its own wealth, people, and God. He needs assurance that Jacob will not return to take revenge, perhaps with Esau’s help, or treat his daughters badly in a distant land where Laban could not intervene. The same pattern appears when Abimelech sought covenants with Abraham and Isaac after seeing that God was with them (Genesis 21:22–23; 26:28–29). In each case the outsider seeks peace with the patriarch because he recognizes God’s blessing on him.

The word “covenant” here refers to a treaty between two human parties, an agreement of mutual non-aggression. It is not the covenant of grace that God made with Abraham, though it borrows the same vocabulary and is sealed with similar rites: a memorial, an oath, a sacrifice, and a meal. The “witness” Laban mentions could refer to the covenant itself or to the memorial that will be set up to commemorate it.

The initiative belongs to Laban, and Jacob simply responds. Jacob does not need the treaty; God has already protected him. Yet he accepts it, because peace with an adversary is worth securing when it can be had honorably. “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Romans 12:18).

wordNotes.term: נִכְרְתָה בְרִית (nikhretah verit) — let us make a covenant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “let us cut a covenant.” The idiom of cutting likely reflects the rites of sacrifice that often accompanied covenant-making. Berit can describe God’s covenants or, as here, treaties between people. The phrase appears in Abraham’s and Isaac’s agreements with Abimelech.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob answers Laban’s proposal with action rather than words: “And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar.” He does not debate the terms. He simply does what he had done at Bethel twenty years before, when he took the stone that had been his pillow and set it up as a memorial (Genesis 28:18).

The two pillars frame Jacob’s years in exile. The first marked the night God met a frightened fugitive and promised to be with him and bring him home. The second marks the day God fulfilled that promise by delivering him from Laban’s hand. Between the two stones lie twenty years of hardship and blessing. Jacob, who had once been carried along by events, now stands as head of a household and sets up a monument on his own initiative.

Standing stones served many purposes in the ancient world. They could mark graves, boundaries, or sacred places, or commemorate agreements. Here the pillar is a witness to a treaty, a silent testimony set on the hill for anyone passing by. Later, Joshua would set up a great stone under an oak at Shechem as a witness to Israel’s covenant with the LORD, saying that the stone had “heard all the words” spoken there (Joshua 24:26–27). The stone could not speak, but it would remind the parties of what had been promised.

The law later forbade Israel to set up pillars as objects of worship in the manner of the Canaanites (Deuteronomy 16:22). Jacob’s pillar was not an idol; it was a memorial, a marker of God’s faithfulness and of an agreement made in his sight. Believers today also need memorials, ways of remembering what God has done, so that they do not forget his past deliverances when new trials come (1 Samuel 7:12).

wordNotes.explanation: From a verb meaning “to stand, set up.” A matstsevah was a standing stone erected as a memorial, boundary marker, or witness. Jacob raises such stones at Bethel, here in Gilead, and at Rachel’s grave. Later law forbade pillars used in idolatrous worship, while memorial stones remained acceptable.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said unto his brethren, Gather stones; and they took stones, and made an heap: and they did eat there upon the heap.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob then turns to “his brethren” and says, “Gather stones.” The kinsmen of both camps gather stones and pile them into a heap. “And they did eat there upon the heap.” Two monuments now stand on the hill: Jacob’s single pillar and the cairn built by the combined company.

“His brethren” probably includes both Jacob’s own men and Laban’s relatives who had come in pursuit. Hours earlier they had been two armed camps facing each other. Now they work side by side and share a meal. The change shows how quickly God can turn hostility into peace when he has restrained the wrath of the aggressor.

The shared meal was an essential part of covenant-making in the ancient world. Eating together signified fellowship, mutual obligation, and peace. Isaac had made a feast for Abimelech when they swore their oath of peace (Genesis 26:30). At Sinai the elders of Israel saw God, “and did eat and drink,” as the covenant was ratified (Exodus 24:11). The table became a sign that enmity had ended.

The Lord’s Supper carries this meaning to its height. At his table Christ gathers former enemies, reconciled to God and to one another through his blood, to eat together as one family (Ephesians 2:13–16; 1 Corinthians 10:17).

wordNotes.explanation: A heap or pile, usually of stones. The word can describe a memorial cairn, as here, or the heap of stones raised over a condemned man like Achan. It forms the first part of the name Galeed in the next verse.

verses.bibleText: And Laban called it Jegarsahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Each man names the heap in his own language. “Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed.” Both names mean the same thing, “heap of witness.” Jegar-sahadutha is Aramaic, the language of Laban’s people; Galeed is Hebrew, the language of Canaan that Jacob’s family spoke.

This is the only Aramaic phrase in the books of Moses, and it marks a turning point. The two branches of Terah’s family have drifted apart not only geographically but culturally and linguistically. One belongs to Aram, the other to the land of promise. The same monument receives two names because it stands between two peoples. By naming it in Hebrew, Jacob identifies himself with Canaan and its covenant future.

The Hebrew name Galeed sounds very like Gilead, the name of the whole region. The narrator has already called the hills “mount Gilead” in anticipation (verses 21, 23, 25). From this event, the area received a name that would endure in Israel’s history. Gilead later became the territory of the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh, and the boundary between Israel and Aram would be fought over many times in the days of the kings (1 Kings 22:3).

The presence of Aramaic in Genesis also reminds us that God’s word reaches across languages. Later, portions of Ezra and Daniel would be written in Aramaic, and Jesus himself spoke Aramaic in his daily ministry (Mark 5:41). The heap in Gilead, with its two names, stands as an early witness that God works among nations and tongues while carrying forward his particular promise through Abraham’s family.

wordNotes.explanation: An Aramaic phrase: yegar means heap, and sahaduta means witness or testimony. It is the earliest Aramaic expression in Scripture. Job uses a related Aramaic word when he says his witness is in heaven.

The Hebrew equivalent: gal, heap, and ‘ed, witness. The name is closely related to Gilead, the region east of the Jordan. The same word ‘ed, witness, recurs in verses 44, 48, 50, and 52, making testimony the theme of the treaty.

verses.bibleText: And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban explains the meaning of the heap: “This heap is a witness between me and thee this day.” He seems to accept Jacob’s Hebrew name, and the narrator adds, “Therefore was the name of it called Galeed.” The stones themselves become a witness, a permanent reminder of the agreement.

The idea that inanimate objects can bear witness appears often in Scripture. Moses called heaven and earth to witness against Israel (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua said the great stone at Shechem had heard the words of the covenant (Joshua 24:27). The point is not that stones listen, but that physical memorials outlast human memory and stand as public evidence of what was promised. Whoever passed this heap in the future would be reminded that a boundary had been set and an oath had been sworn.

“This day” fixes the moment. Laban and Jacob are formally ending the long dispute and setting a new relationship on record. In Scripture, covenant days are remembered. What God and people promise on a particular day becomes a reference point for generations. Christians, too, look back to a day when they publicly entered into covenant with God in baptism, a day meant to be remembered.

wordNotes.explanation: A witness who testifies to what he has seen or heard. In covenant contexts the witness can be a person, God himself, or a monument that serves as lasting evidence. The word appears repeatedly in this treaty scene, underscoring its legal character.

verses.bibleText: And Mizpah; for he said, The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The place receives another name: “And Mizpah; for he said, The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.” Mizpah means “watchtower” or “lookout point.” Laban calls on the LORD to keep watch over both parties once they have parted and can no longer see each other.

These words have often been used as a tender farewell between friends or loved ones, engraved on jewelry and spoken at partings. That use can be sweet, but it is not what Laban meant. In context the “Mizpah benediction” is closer to a warning. Laban does not trust Jacob, and Jacob does not trust Laban. Since neither can watch the other across hundreds of miles, they ask God to act as the watchman who sees what each does and holds each accountable. The words are a solemn appeal to divine oversight between suspicious parties.

It is striking that Laban uses the covenant name of God, the LORD, here. He had learned it from Abraham’s servant (Genesis 24:31) and had felt its power in his dream. Laban may have viewed the LORD as Jacob’s family deity, the one most likely to bind Jacob’s conscience. Either way, he acknowledges that the God of Jacob sees everything, even when human eyes cannot.

The truth Laban invokes is real, even if his motive is mixed. God does watch. “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3). For the guilty, this is a sobering warning; for the faithful, it is comfort. The same God who sees wrongdoing in secret also sees the obedience and suffering of his people in secret and will reward them openly (Matthew 6:4). The place called Mizpah in Gilead appears later in Israel’s history. Jephthah, the judge, lived there and made his vows before the LORD at Mizpah (Judges 11:11, 34). The name given at this parting remained in the land as a reminder that God watches over agreements made in his name.

There is a gentle lesson for those who apply this verse at partings today. The comfort is not merely that God watches over those we love when we are absent, though he does. It is that he watches over our own conduct too, and we must live as people who know we are seen.

wordNotes.explanation: From tsafah, “to watch, keep watch, look out.” A mitspah is a watchpost or lookout. Several places in Israel bore the name, including this one in Gilead and another in Benjamin where Samuel judged Israel. The name expresses the idea of God’s watchful oversight.

wordNotes.term: יִצֶף יְהוָה (yitsef YHWH) — the LORD watch
wordNotes.explanation: A wish or prayer that the LORD would keep watch. The verb, related to Mizpah, describes a sentinel’s alert watching. Ezekiel was appointed a “watchman” using a related noun. Laban asks God to be the sentinel over the treaty.

verses.bibleText: If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take other wives beside my daughters, no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban lays out his first condition: “If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take other wives beside my daughters, no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee.” He fears that Jacob, once beyond his reach, might mistreat Rachel and Leah or take additional wives who would compete with them and their children for Jacob’s affection and inheritance.

The irony is heavy. Laban had himself afflicted his daughters by selling them and devouring their bride price (verse 15). He had created the very polygamy he now worries about by forcing two sisters on one husband. Now he poses as their protector. Yet the concern itself was legitimate. In the ancient world, a woman far from her father’s house had few defenders. Marriage contracts from the region sometimes included clauses forbidding a husband to take another wife, and Laban’s condition reflects that kind of protection.

The word “afflict” is the same verb later used for the Egyptian oppression of Israel (Exodus 1:11–12) and for the mistreatment of widows and orphans that God forbids (Exodus 22:22–23). God hears the cry of the afflicted, especially those without human defenders.

“No man is with us; see, God is witness.” No human court could enforce this treaty across the distance that would separate them. Only God could see whether Jacob kept his word. Laban appeals to the One who sees in secret. Scripture records that Jacob did not take other wives; his household after this point consists of the four women already in it. Malachi would later remind Israel that the LORD is witness between a man and the wife of his youth (Malachi 2:14).

wordNotes.explanation: From ‘anah in an intensive form, “to oppress, humble, mistreat.” It describes Sarah’s harsh treatment of Hagar and Egypt’s oppression of Israel. Laban uses it to forbid any abuse of his daughters.

verses.bibleText: And Laban said to Jacob, Behold this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Laban said to Jacob, Behold this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee.” Laban points to both monuments and claims them as his own work. Yet the narrative has told us that Jacob set up the pillar (verse 45) and that Jacob directed the gathering of the heap (verse 46). Laban speaks as though he had done it all.

The claim is typical of the man. Laban habitually takes credit and property that belong to others. He claimed Jacob’s wives, children, and flocks as his own (verse 43), and now he claims Jacob’s pillar. It is a small detail, but it shows that the covenant has not changed Laban’s character. He still speaks as the master of everything in sight.

The double “behold” draws attention to the physical evidence, as a speaker in a legal setting might point to exhibits. Laban wants the stones to speak for him in the future. Jacob lets the claim pass without protest. He has already said what needed to be said in verses 36–42, and he does not need to win every point. There is wisdom in knowing when an argument has been settled and further words would only stir up strife (Proverbs 17:14; 26:4).

wordNotes.explanation: From yarah, which can mean to throw or shoot, and also to set or lay down, as in laying a foundation or cornerstone. Laban uses it of setting up the stone monuments. The same verb describes God laying the cornerstone of the earth.

verses.bibleText: This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness, that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap and this pillar unto me, for harm.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban states the second condition, the heart of the treaty: “This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness, that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap and this pillar unto me, for harm.” The monuments mark a boundary. Neither party may cross it with hostile intent.

The clause “for harm” is important. The treaty did not forbid all travel or contact; it forbade crossing the line to do injury. Laban was concerned that Jacob, growing in wealth and possibly allied with Esau, might one day come north to take revenge. Jacob, for his part, needed assurance that Laban would not mount another raid. The stones settled both fears.

The agreement anticipates the later political boundary between Israel and Aram. In the days of the kings, the region of Gilead was repeatedly contested between the two nations (1 Kings 22:3; 2 Kings 10:32–33). The heap on the hill marked a frontier that would be remembered, and too often crossed, by their descendants. A treaty between two men became a picture of relations between two peoples.

The principle remains wise for relationships today. Where trust has been broken and reconciliation is limited, clear boundaries can preserve peace. Paul could part from Barnabas over a sharp disagreement and still later speak well of Mark (Acts 15:39; 2 Timothy 4:11). Separation without hostility is sometimes the best that can be achieved, and God can work through it.

wordNotes.explanation: From ra‘ah, “evil, harm, calamity.” The preposition indicates purpose: crossing with intent to do harm. It links back to Laban’s claim in verse 29 that he had power to do Jacob “hurt,” using the related verb. The treaty renounces that power.

verses.bibleText: The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban invokes divine judges: “The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us.” He names three: the God of Abraham, Jacob’s grandfather; the God of Nahor, Laban’s grandfather; and the God of their father, Terah, who was father to both Abraham and Nahor. Laban appeals to the shared family heritage that reached back before the two lines divided.

The question is whether Laban had one God in view or several. The verb “judge” in the Hebrew text is plural, which may suggest that Laban thought of distinct deities, one for each branch of the family. Joshua reminded Israel that Terah and Nahor “served other gods” beyond the river (Joshua 24:2), and Laban’s own household gods show that idolatry was present in his home. Yet the family of Nahor had also retained some knowledge of the true God, which is why Laban could speak of the LORD (Genesis 24:31, 50; 31:49). Several ancient translations render the verb as singular, treating the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor as one. Laban probably held a blurred, mixed faith in which the LORD was acknowledged alongside other powers.

Jacob removes all ambiguity: “And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.” He does not swear by the God of Nahor or of Terah. He swears by the God whom his father Isaac revered, the God of the covenant who had revealed himself at Bethel and had just protected him from Laban. Whatever Laban meant, Jacob’s oath is bound to the one true God.

This moment teaches that a shared ancestry does not guarantee a shared faith. Abraham and Nahor came from the same household, but only Abraham answered God’s call to leave the gods of Mesopotamia. Their descendants stood on the same hill but swore by different names. True faith is not inherited automatically; each generation must choose whom it will serve (Joshua 24:15).

The distinction also guards against a vague religion that treats all gods as equal. Jacob did not accept Laban’s blending of the LORD with other deities. The first commandment would later make the principle explicit: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3). Swearing by the LORD alone was an act of loyalty that set Jacob apart from his relatives in Aram.

wordNotes.explanation: From shafat, “to judge, decide, govern.” The form is plural, “may they judge,” which can imply more than one deity in Laban’s mind, although some ancient versions read a singular. Abraham had appealed to “the Judge of all the earth,” using the same root.

From shava‘, “to swear an oath.” An oath called God to witness and invoked judgment on the one who broke it. Israel was commanded to swear only by the LORD’s name, and Jacob’s choice of the Fear of Isaac follows that principle.

verses.bibleText: Then Jacob offered sacrifice upon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread: and they did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Jacob offered sacrifice upon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread: and they did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.” Jacob seals the covenant with worship. He offers a sacrifice to the God by whom he had sworn and then hosts a meal for all the kinsmen.

This is the first sacrifice Jacob is recorded as offering. At Bethel he had set up a pillar and poured oil on it, but there is no mention of an animal offering there. Now, on the heights of Gilead, he acts as the priest of his household, as Abraham and Isaac had done before him (Genesis 22:13; 26:25). The sacrifice is an act of thanksgiving for deliverance and a solemn ratification of the oath he has sworn. It is offered to the LORD alone, not to the gods Laban had named.

The type of sacrifice described here is one in which the worshipers ate part of the offering, sharing a meal in God’s presence. Such sacrifices expressed fellowship with God and with one another. They anticipate the peace offerings of the later sanctuary, in which the offerer and his family ate before the LORD (Leviticus 7:15–16). All such offerings drew their meaning from the sacrifice to which they pointed: Christ, through whom peace is made between God and humanity and between divided people (Colossians 1:20).

“They did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.” The night before, two hostile camps had pitched their tents against each other with hammers sounding. This night, they sleep side by side after a shared meal. The change came not from Jacob’s cunning or Laban’s goodwill, but from the intervention of God, who had spoken to Laban in a dream. God brought peace where there had been the threat of bloodshed.

The scene also prepares for the even greater reconciliation that lies ahead. Jacob has made peace with Laban; he must still face Esau. The God who turned the night of confrontation in Gilead into a night of peace would go before him to Peniel and beyond.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb and noun from the same root emphasize the act: “he sacrificed a sacrifice.” A zevach was typically an animal slaughtered as an offering, part of which was eaten by the worshipers in a communal meal. It is the term later used for peace offerings and covenant meals.

Literally “bread,” but often used for food or a meal in general. To “eat bread” together was to share table fellowship and, in a covenant setting, to confirm peace. The phrase appears when Melchizedek brought bread and when Joseph ate with his brothers.

verses.bibleText: And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place.” In the Hebrew Bible this verse opens chapter 32, but in the English versions it closes the story of Jacob and Laban.

Laban gets his wish from verse 28. He kisses his grandchildren and his daughters farewell. There is no record that he kissed Jacob, although he had run to embrace and kiss him when they first met twenty years earlier (Genesis 29:13). The men part as treaty partners, not as affectionate kin. Their relationship has been preserved from violence, but not restored to warmth.

Laban also blesses his daughters and grandchildren. Whatever his faults, he sends them off with words of good will, as his family had once blessed Rebekah when she left for Canaan (Genesis 24:60). Perhaps the covenant meal, the presence of his grandchildren, and the knowledge that he would not see them again softened his heart. Scripture does not tell us. The blessing, at any rate, closes the scene on a note of peace.

“And Laban departed, and returned unto his place.” With this, Laban disappears from the biblical narrative. The family in Canaan and the family in Aram go their separate ways, and contact between them ceases. Laban returns to Haran and his gods; Jacob goes forward to Canaan and to the God of Bethel. The parting is a quiet but decisive moment. The covenant line has been separated from the old world of Mesopotamia once and for all.

The next verse begins with angels of God meeting Jacob on the way (Genesis 32:1). Laban leaves; heavenly messengers arrive. The man who had shadowed Jacob’s life for twenty years exits, and the hosts of God appear to escort him toward the even greater challenge of meeting Esau. Those who walk in God’s path find that when one chapter of trouble closes, God is already present for the next.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּשְׁכֵּם (wayyashkem) — and early in the morning … rose up
wordNotes.explanation: From shakam, “to rise early.” The verb often marks the start of a significant action or journey undertaken without delay. Abraham rose early to go to Moriah; Jacob rose early at Bethel. Here it signals Laban’s prompt departure after the treaty.

Literally “to his place,” meaning his home or territory. The phrase marks a definitive return and separation. It is used of Balaam returning home after failing to curse Israel, signaling that his role in the story is over.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How do we tell the difference between a hard season God is using and a season God is calling us to leave?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God who promised at Bethel to be with Jacob kept that promise through twenty years of unjust treatment, called him home, restrained his enemy, and proved himself the living God beside powerless household idols.
discussionQuestions: Why does Jacob credit God in verses 5–13 with what chapter 30 described as his own breeding strategy?
What do Rachel’s theft and concealment of the images reveal about the spiritual condition of Jacob’s household?
How does Jacob’s description of his shepherding in verses 38–40 compare with the work of the Good Shepherd in John 10?
Why might Laban, rather than Jacob, be the one who needed a covenant?
What does the chapter teach about leaving a hostile relationship without seeking revenge?
commonMisunderstandings: Mizpah (verse 49) was spoken between two suspicious men as a warning, not as a tender farewell between friends.
God’s protection of Jacob does not approve every method Jacob used; grace carries him despite his flaws.
Rachel’s idols were not a harmless keepsake; their later burial at Shechem shows they had to be put away.
The custom of women in verse 35 does not make a woman sinful; it concerns ceremonial uncleanness later regulated in the law.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the focus on God’s faithfulness: he speaks first, he sees Laban’s injustice, he restrains the pursuer, and he is the witness who watches when the parties are out of each other’s sight.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Trust the God who has seen your labor and your affliction, obey his call even when it means leaving what is familiar, and put away every rival god you have been carrying.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The living God keeps his promises, sees the afflicted, and calls his people out of bondage to himself, while idols prove helpless.
flow: Jacob served twenty years in a house of hard bondage, cheated again and again.
God saw his affliction, prospered him, and called him home with the promise “I will be with thee.”
Laban’s gods could neither protect themselves nor be found; the God of Jacob restrained the pursuer.
Jacob’s faithful, sleepless shepherding points to Christ, who laid down his life for the sheep.
God calls each person to leave rival gods and follow him toward the promised inheritance.
simpleIllustrations: A god that has to be hidden in a saddle bag and sat upon cannot carry anyone; the living God carries his people (Isaiah 46:4).
A boundary cairn on a hillside marked the end of a feud; the cross marks the place where God himself made peace.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you answer God’s call to return to him, leaving behind whatever rival you have been carrying with you?
cautions: Do not turn Jacob into a flawless hero; the text shows deception on every side.
Do not use Mizpah as a sentimental blessing without explaining its original setting.
Do not suggest that hardship always means God wants a person to leave; Jacob waited for God’s word.

reflectionQuestions: Where have I mistaken my own cleverness for the source of blessings God has given me?
Is there an idol I am carrying with me, hidden but still cherished, that God is asking me to put away?
How do I respond when I am treated unjustly by someone with more power than I have?
Do I wait for God’s direction before making major moves, or do I let pressure alone decide?
Whom do I need to leave in God’s hands as witness and judge instead of seeking to settle the account myself?
